details: ADK Go's loop runs entirely in your Go process via runner.Runner.Run → llminternal.Flow.Run with no subprocess, sidecar, or vendor bridge. The same module also ships an optional first-party HTTP/SSE/WebSocket/A2A server that embeds the loop in the same OS process. This is the simplest deployment shape of any benchmarked stack.

Agno's loop is a single Python _run/_arun function in agno.agent._run executed inside your Python (FastAPI) process. AgentOS mounts 50+ routes against the same in-process agent — no subprocess, no vendor cloud required. Background memory/learning work runs as threads or asyncio tasks in the same process.

AutoAgents runs the loop in the caller's tokio runtime: BaseAgent::run → AgentExecutor::execute → TurnEngine::run_turn, all inside the host Rust process. There is no daemon, subprocess, or vendor cloud. An optional ractor-based actor runtime is in-process pub/sub only.

The actual agent loop (turn boundaries, tool dispatch, planner, hook firing, compaction) runs in the bundled Claude Code Node.js CLI spawned via subprocess over a JSON control protocol. The Python side is a transport + typed-message parser + hook callback router. You cannot fork the loop without forking Claude Code.

note: 3 — TS shim over native CLI binary
details: Despite the TypeScript SDK branding, the agent loop executes in a spawned native Claude Code binary (~200MB per platform), not in your Node process. The TS code is a transport + control-protocol shim over stdio JSON-RPC. Architectural ceiling is identical to the Python SDK — you cannot escape the Claude Code subprocess.

CrewAI runs the loop in your Python process: Crew.kickoff → AgentExecutor (a Flow subclass with planning, todo list, asyncio.gather parallel step execution). No subprocess, no separate runtime, no vendor binary — the library is the loop. LLM HTTP calls go directly from the same process to the provider.

Eino's loop runs in your Go binary in a goroutine spawned by ChatModelAgent.Run, driving a compiled compose.Graph internally. Workflow agents fan out via real sync.WaitGroup goroutines. No subprocess, no vendor daemon, no hosted service — purely in-process import-and-call.

Genkit Go's loop is a single in-process Go function — ai.GenerateWithRequest — that recursively calls the model, runs tool calls, and feeds results back until done. No subprocess, no IPC, no remote agent runner. The genkit-tools JS CLI talks to your process only in dev mode via a Reflection HTTP server.

The graph runtime runs inside PregelLoop.tick() in your Python process — tools, checkpointer I/O, and LLM calls all execute in-process. The closed-source langgraph_api HTTP server wraps the same in-process loop but adds queue + persistence + auth on top; that's a paid platform layer, not where the loop lives.

LlamaIndex's agent layer runs as an asyncio coroutine inside your Python process. FunctionAgent.run resolves into Workflow.run which schedules @step methods on the running event loop. No bundled binary, no subprocess, no vendor cloud round-trip.

Mastra's loop runs entirely in your Node/Bun/Edge process: the loop is itself a Mastra workflow (then(llmExecutionStep).foreach(toolCallStep)…). No subprocess, no vendor binary. The Hono-based @mastra/server embeds the agent in the same process.

MAF runs the loop in-process: Python BaseChatClient.get_response and .NET FunctionInvokingChatClient middleware both execute the LLM round-trip and tool-call loop in the host process. No subprocesses, no bundled CLIs. Optional hosted runtimes (Azure Functions, DurableTask, Foundry) externalize orchestration when chosen.

openai-agents runs Runner.run as a single-threaded async loop on your asyncio event loop. The entire ReAct loop — including streaming, tool dispatch, guardrail evaluation, hook firing, and session persistence — happens inside your Python process. No bundled CLI, no Node sidecar, no sister-repo server.

Runner.run is a TypeScript while(true) loop inside your Node/Deno/Bun process that calls a Model instance over HTTP/SSE/WebSocket directly. No subprocess, no vendor binary, no first-party server. The OpenAI in the name is provider-agnostic loop + first-party OpenAI provider.

Agent.run opens a pydantic_graph GraphRun walking UserPromptNode → ModelRequestNode → CallToolsNode → End in your Python process. Every model call is model.request(...) executed by the host — no bundled binary, no subprocess, no vendor cloud. HTTP exposure is opt-in via agent.to_web() or UI adapters.

Rig is a Rust library: the agent loop lives in the caller's Tokio runtime as plain async functions in crates/rig-core/src/agent/prompt_request/. No bundled server, no sidecar process, no vendor cloud — pure Cargo crates you pull into your binary.

Strands runs the loop in your Python process as a pure-Python async generator (event_loop_cycle in src/strands/event_loop/event_loop.py). No subprocess, no bundled binary, no vendor cloud. Closer to LangGraph/Vercel AI SDK style than to Claude Agent SDK Python.

Agent.stream() is an async function* generator running entirely inside the host Node.js (or browser) process on the V8 event loop. No bundled server, no subprocess, no vendor runtime. An optional A2A Express adapter exposes any agent as a JSON-RPC endpoint without changing where the loop runs.

The agent loop runs inside generateText / streamText as a do/while loop in your Node.js process. ToolLoopAgent is a thin wrapper around that — not a long-running process. No vendor cloud, no subprocess, no daemon — only LLM provider HTTPS calls leave the process.

Go 1.25 binary with pure-Go modules (google.golang.org/genai, gorilla/mux, gorm). No bundled binaries, no native libs, no mandatory Postgres or Redis, no mandatory Vertex — runs on Gemini API key alone. Optional GORM driver of your choice (Postgres/Spanner/SQLite); Vertex/GCS only if you choose those backends.

Python 3.7+; for the AgentOS server: fastapi[standard] + uvicorn + sqlalchemy + PyJWT + opentelemetry-sdk + openinference-instrumentation-agno + croniter + pytz. Optional DB driver of your choice. Moderate footprint — pydantic v2 + 100+ tool modules + 49 model adapters baked in.

Rust 1.75+ with tokio runtime; ractor for actor runtime. No mandatory database, no Redis, no Postgres, no LangSmith. Every LLM provider, vector store, sandbox (wasmtime/Deno/rquickjs), and MCP client is gated behind a Cargo feature so you only pay for what you use.

Python 3.10+ wheel ships a Claude Code Node.js binary under src/claude_agent_sdk/_bundled/claude (platform-specific). Requires anyio, sniffio, mcp>=1.23, and an Anthropic API key for the subprocess. The bundled artifact makes the wheel chunky and platform-specific.

Node ≥18 (or Bun/Deno), plus mandatory optionalDependency on a per-platform Claude Code binary of 207–233 MB. Multi-arch Docker images install all matching binaries (~460 MB for linux-x64 + linux-arm64 under npm). Also requires @anthropic-ai/sdk + @modelcontextprotocol/sdk + zod as peer deps and optional bubblewrap for sandboxing.

Python 3.10–3.13. Hard deps: crewai-core, crewai-cli, pydantic>=2.11, openai>=2.30, instructor, pdfplumber, regex, opentelemetry-api/sdk, chromadb. Optional: provider SDKs, mcp, e2b/daytona, lancedb, aiosqlite. No bundled binaries; LanceDB writes to ./.memory/ and checkpoints to ./.checkpoints by default.

Go 1.25; small set of direct deps (sonic JSON, kin-openapi, gonja templates, testify). No bundled binaries, no native libs, no required external process. Provider adapters (LLMs, vector stores, tracing) ship as separate eino-ext Go modules so you import only what you need.

note: 4 — Go modules; optional JS CLI for dev
details: Go ≥1.25 with no bundled binaries — everything is pure-Go modules. Optional Node.js + genkit CLI for the dev UI/eval (not in your production binary). Optional GCP credentials, OTel exporter, or Postgres/Firestore depending on plugins chosen.

Python ≥3.10. Core: langchain-core, langgraph-checkpoint, langgraph-sdk, langgraph-prebuilt, xxhash, pydantic. Optional storage backends via separate packages (langgraph-checkpoint-postgres, langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite). LLM providers BYO via langchain-* packages. HTTP server requires closed-source langgraph-runtime-inmem/postgres.

Python 3.10+. Core pulls SQLAlchemy[asyncio], httpx, pydantic>=2.8, tiktoken, aiohttp, nltk, tenacity, wrapt, banks, aiosqlite, llama-index-workflows. No bundled binaries; tokenizer is tiktoken. Each LLM/store/tool integration adds its own provider SDK dependency from ~300 separately-versioned packages.

Node.js ≥18 (or Bun/Cloudflare Workers/Vercel Edge), pnpm for dev. Default in-memory store must be replaced for production with @mastra/store-libsql/-pg/etc. Optional vector store, Redis pubsub, OTel/Datadog. The package itself is heavy (>200 source files, packages/core/src/agent/agent.ts is ~7k lines).

Python: pydantic, mcp, opentelemetry-*, httpx, python-dotenv + provider extras (openai/anthropic/azure-identity). .NET: Microsoft.Extensions.AI, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging, OpenTelemetry.* + provider SDKs. Optional backing stores via agent-framework-redis, agent-framework-azure-cosmos, Azure AI Search.

Python 3.10+. Core deps: openai>=2.26, pydantic>=2.12, griffelib, typing-extensions, requests, websockets, mcp. No bundled binaries, no native libs beyond pydantic-core wheels. Optional extras for litellm, redis, dapr, mongodb, docker, sandbox providers, etc.

Node.js 22+ (Deno/Bun also supported; Cloudflare Workers experimental). Direct deps: openai SDK, debug, optional zod, optional @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. No bundled DB. For default tracing: outbound HTTPS to platform.openai.com.

Required: Python 3.10+, pydantic/pydantic-core/pydantic-graph, genai-prices, opentelemetry-*, anyio. Per-provider SDKs are optional extras (openai/anthropic/google/mistral/groq/cohere/bedrock/xai/huggingface). No required databases or queues; durable execution opts in via temporal/dbos/prefect/restate extras.

Rust edition 2024 with Tokio runtime. HTTP client configurable (defaults reqwest). 26 native provider crates plus 10+ vector-store companion crates, each gated by Cargo features. WASM-compatible (`wasm_compat.rs`). No mandatory DB.

Python ≥3.10. Mandatory: boto3, botocore, docstring_parser, jsonschema, mcp, pydantic, pyyaml, watchdog, opentelemetry-api/sdk/instrumentation-threading. Bedrock default. Optional extras for anthropic, gemini, litellm, llamaapi, mistral, ollama, openai, writer, sagemaker, a2a, bidi.

Node ≥20. Required: @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime, uuid, yaml, @types/json-schema (only Bedrock client is non-trivial). All other providers (Anthropic/OpenAI/Google/Vercel/MCP/Express/A2A/S3/OTel) are optional peer-deps you install if you use them. Browser-bundle tested in CI.

Node v18/20/22 (v22 recommended). pnpm v10+ for dev. No native libs required, no database required by the SDK. Optional LLM provider account and/or Vercel AI Gateway. Frontend adapters for React/Vue/Svelte/Angular/RSC are separate first-party packages.

note: 4 — Cloud Run, one process per app
details: README explicitly recommends containerization and Cloud Run; cmd/launcher/full composes Web UI + REST + A2A + agent-engine emulator into a single Go binary. Pattern is one binary per app deployed as Cloud Run service or GKE deployment, with sessions in Cloud SQL or Vertex Agent Engine. Multi-tenant achieved by namespacing on (AppName, UserID, SessionID).

Canonical pattern is agent_os.serve(app=run:app) which calls uvicorn.run with one process serving many concurrent sessions and many agents. Auth, RBAC, scheduling, tracing are all handled inside this single process. AgentOS provides 50+ endpoints, JWT scopes, RBAC scopes, scheduler, traces, knowledge — production-shaped out of the box.

Docs describe direct vs actor agent shapes but do not prescribe container-per-tenant vs shared process. You embed AutoAgents in whatever Rust binary you build — Axum/Actix/custom. README's Performance section says scalable via multi-agent coordination but refers to in-process actor runtime, not multi-process deployment.

Not stated in the SDK repo. Implicit: every query()/ClaudeSDKClient spawns a new claude subprocess; natural shape is container-per-tenant or one-Python-process-many-CLI-subprocesses-but-one-CLI-per-active-conversation. Repo ships Dockerfile.test for CI but no production Dockerfile or hosted runtime.

Vendor hosting doc recommends one CLI subprocess per session mediated by your HTTP server. attachBridgeSession and runAssistantWorker (alpha) document a worker-per-session pattern with userIdleMs despawn. For pure server-side multi-tenant the practical topology is N session workers per pod each owning one CLI subprocess. No first-party queue or scheduler.

OSS docs assume one Python process running a Crew per request. AMP (Enterprise) recommends GitHub-or-ZIP deploy to their managed runtime where containers spin per crew per automation. No vendor guidance on container-per-tenant vs one-process-many-tenants for the OSS path because OSS has no tenant primitive. production-architecture page discusses crew design patterns, not horizontal scaling.

No vendor-recommended topology document — this is a library, not a platform. CloudWeGo docs implicitly assume one-process-many-tenants with horizontal Pod scaling and BYO ingress; multi-tenancy guidance is minimal. Used inside ByteDance with each Pod owning persistence; equivalent guidance externally lives in user-side platforms.

Go SDK and samples all show one Go binary serving N HTTP routes, each a genkit.Handler(action). samples/cloud_run_deploy.sh targets Google Cloud Run as the canonical hosting model — stateless container instances behind a load balancer. Sessions and conversation state explicitly punted to your DB; tenant identity flows via headers → ContextProvider → core.WithActionContext.

LangGraph Platform docs recommend one-process-many-tenants with horizontal scaling: a fleet of API pods sharing Postgres for state + Redis for pub/sub between API and worker pods. Self-host follows the same pattern (langgraph up Docker compose, K8s Helm chart). Pure-OSS deployments without Platform are BYO HTTP layer.

Not opinionated. The official deployment tutorial at docs/src/content/docs/framework/understanding/deployment/deployment.md literally says TODO. The vendor's recommended path for production multi-agent serving is the separate llama_deploy project (microservice / message-queue runtime around Workflow), which is out of scope of the core repo.

Recommended pattern is one-process-many-tenants: single Mastra instance with all agents/workflows/tools registered at boot; @mastra/server is stateless across requests with state in the storage backend. Deployers under deployers/ package this for Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Workers, plus deployers/cloud for Mastra Cloud. Resumable streams make session affinity unnecessary.

Vendor documents multiple options with explicit samples: one-process-many-tenants via Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting (AddAIAgent + AgentSessionStore + AIHostAgent for ASP.NET Core / Worker Service); container-per-agent via Foundry Hosted Agents; worker pool / durable orchestration via Microsoft.Agents.AI.DurableTask and Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting.AzureFunctions. .NET hosting story maps cleanly onto multi-tenant servers.

note: 2 — uniform one-process examples, no vendor opinion
details: SDK has no vendor opinion on topology. Examples uniformly assume one Python process per host hosting many sessions via asyncio. For horizontal scaling: run N stateless worker processes with a shared store (Postgres via SQLAlchemySession, Redis via RedisSession, MongoDB via MongoDBSession). Each worker can serve any session as long as it can reach the store.

Docs do not prescribe a topology. examples/nextjs reference shows one-process-many-requests embedded in a Next.js Route Handler. Each run() call is request-scoped. Many concurrent runs share one Node process but each owns its own RunState. No built-in worker pool, queue, or cluster mode. Cloudflare Workers documented as experimental.

Not explicitly opinionated; docs treat Agent like a FastAPI app: "Agents are designed for reuse, like FastAPI Apps". UI adapter docs assume one agent instance per ASGI app and one HTTP route per agent endpoint. Production durable patterns are documented for Temporal/DBOS/Prefect via durable_execution extras.

Not opinionated. Rig is a library; the docs offer no production deployment guidance. You ship a Rust binary (typically axum + tokio) and embed Rig inside it. Container-per-tenant vs. one-process-many-tenants is your call.

Not prescribed by the SDK itself but there is an official strandsagents.com docs page for operating agents in production. The hard _invocation_lock that refuses concurrent invocations on a single Agent effectively pushes you toward one Agent instance per active session. No queue/worker primitives in-tree.

Not prescribed in the repo. README and examples treat the SDK as a normal Node library. A host typically would put new Agent(...) instances behind an HTTP layer (Express/Hono/Fastify) — there is no shipped agent runtime daemon. Optional A2A Express server is for inter-agent comms, not user-facing chat.

SDK doesn't ship hosting recipes but Vercel docs and examples/next-agent recommend mounting createAgentUIStreamResponse inside a Next.js API route — one process per Node instance, many tenants per process. For multi-region you scale Next.js horizontally, but all session state lives in your external DB (no in-process session map).

note: 5 — Go binary, sub-second start, tens of MB
details: Sub-second from main() to first r.Run(...) (Go binary linking + genai.NewClient HTTPS handshake). RAM baseline tens of MB; disk ~20–40 MB depending on whether you embed the Web UI. No equivalent of Claude Agent SDK's 20–30s startup. Fastest cold-start of any benchmarked stack.

Cold start = Python interpreter import + FastAPI app + AgentOS init (db lifespan initialises sync and async databases). With Postgres-backed BaseDb this includes SQLAlchemy engine creation and optional table creation/migration. Exact RAM/disk not measured but moderate footprint from pydantic v2 + 100+ tool modules + 49 model adapters.

Release binary cold start is essentially process startup time (typically <100 ms). Memory baseline is small with no embedded vector store and no LLM weights unless you opt into llama.cpp/mistral-rs features. Compile time is the real cost — full workspace builds with all features are significant.

Each connect() runs _check_claude_version (2s timeout), anyio.open_process for the CLI binary, then an initialize control-protocol roundtrip (default 60s timeout, configurable). Empirically a few seconds to ready; cold-start latency is dominated by Node startup. Issue #333 reports 20–30s cold start for some configurations. ~200–500 MB RAM per active session.

Binary footprint 207–233 MB per platform in node_modules. Cold start per subprocess estimated 5–20s warm-process resolve + initialize handshake; the startup()/WarmQuery API exists to amortize this. Per-session RAM baseline ~1 GB resident (issue #268 reports listSessions() alone using 900 MB+). Heaviest of all benchmarked stacks by bytes-on-disk.

Fresh import crewai + Crew.kickoff() is dominated by openai + LiteLLM imports (~0.5–1 s on cold disk) and LanceDB index initialization (~100 ms). No 20–30s startup penalty like Claude Agent SDK. RAM baseline ~150 MB Python interpreter + framework, growing with memory store size.

Startup latency is negligible (Runner construction is struct allocation, adk/runner.go:63-69) — no model warm-up, no checkpoint hydration, no plugin loading. Per-session memory is dominated by runSession.Events accumulating during a run. Disk baseline zero (no on-disk cache, no JSONL persistence, no skill cache unless you build one). Massive cold-start advantage for serverless deployments.

Init cost dominated by plugin Init(ctx) calls (googlegenai.Init is sync HTTP/credential check, typically <1s with cached ADC). Go binaries cold-boot ≪1 s after image pull on Cloud Run. RAM baseline ~30 MB for a minimal binary, growing with model SDKs (Vertex AI client + gRPC adds ~50 MB on first call). No 20–30s startup ceremony.

Pure-OSS embedding has a few hundred ms to import the package and RAM baseline a few tens of MB beyond your model client. LangGraph Platform / self-host: Starlette+Uvicorn worker pods with multi-tenant Postgres connection pool dominating RAM (closed-source server, exact numbers not visible).

Pure-Python import overhead — llama-index-core pulls in SQLAlchemy, pydantic, tiktoken, nltk, banks, httpx, aiohttp (non-trivial). No published baseline RAM figure. Cold start is dominated by your LLM SDK warm-up, not the framework itself.

No public benchmark in-repo. Processor pipeline and registry are lazy-instantiated, but @mastra/core is heavy (>200 source files). Realistic baseline for a 5-agent app: tens of MB RAM, sub-second cold start on Node, longer (~1–2 s) on Cloudflare Workers due to bundle size.

Not advertised explicitly. The framework is a thin .NET assembly / Python package — startup is dominated by provider SDK initialization (AzureCliCredential, OpenAIClient) and any context-provider loading (e.g. scanning skill directories). DevUI lists ports 8080/8090; not for production.

Cold start is low — import agents triggers a chain of openai SDK + pydantic imports; lazy SQLiteSession import. No 20–30s startup like Claude Agent SDK. RAM baseline modest (~100–150 MB for Python interpreter + pydantic + openai SDK). Disk baseline tens of MB; SQLiteSession defaults to :memory: (zero disk) unless pointed at a file.

No bundled binary — the SDK is pure JS/TS so startup is whatever your Node process takes (~200–400 ms typical). RAM baseline minimal beyond Node baseline; sessions live in memory by default (MemorySession). No equivalent of Claude Agent SDK issue #333 (slow bootstrap).

Pure-Python import — sub-second once Python interpreter is warm. No bundled binaries, no LLM subprocess. RAM baseline = whatever pydantic + the chosen provider SDK brings. Cold start dominated by Python and provider SDK imports, not by pydantic-ai itself.

Rust binary startup typically <500 ms once compiled (no JIT, no Python interpreter). No vendor binary downloaded; no Node sidecar. Memory baseline small — the Agent struct is a few Arcs plus a tokio::sync::RwLock-wrapped ToolServerState.

Construction is light — Agent.__init__ initializes ToolRegistry, HookRegistry, EventLoopMetrics, OTel tracer. Cold start is dominated by Python-import cost from boto3/pydantic. No 20–30 s subprocess warm-up like Claude Agent SDK Python.

Not measured but expected to be light because no subprocess starts. Lazy-loaded peer-deps mean tree-shaken bundles can stay small. The browser bundle check in CI suggests modest baseline footprint. WASM build exists for the strands-py Python guest runtime.

Cold start of ai itself is just a JS import — typically tens of milliseconds. No bundled binaries or large native deps. Footprint is essentially Node's baseline. The first LLM call is dominated by the provider's API latency, not the SDK.
